answer: A reputation system can require each agent to post a refundable bond before it may influence a shared market, then slash that bond when its signed actions violate a verifiable rule, such as submitting conflicting bids. Reputation accrues slowly from consistent behavior, so a newcomer cannot cheaply create many trusted identities at once. The bond might be backed by shale, onyx, or timber claims, but each identity still ties up scarce value: an attacker pays the capital cost repeatedly and risks losing it when caught.
